parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what impedance controls in a circuit - if the impedance at the two op-amp inputs is extremely large, what does that imply for any current trying to flow into them?
parts.proper_answer: No current flows into either input of the op-amp.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Input Impedance Means**
Think of impedance as resistance to alternating or direct current. A very large impedance blocks current flow, just like a very large resistor.

Step 2: **Apply To Ideal Op-amp**
For an ideal op-amp the input impedance is infinite, so even with a voltage between the inputs, the current drawn is zero. That is $$I_{in} = 0$$ at both the inverting (-) and non-inverting (+) inputs.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Recall that bandwidth describes the range of frequencies an amplifier can handle - what would it mean if that range had no limit?
parts.proper_answer: The voltage gain remains constant for all frequencies of input signal.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Bandwidth Means**
A real op-amp amplifies well only up to a certain frequency, after which the gain falls. Bandwidth is the range of frequencies over which gain stays high.

Step 2: **Apply To Ideal Op-amp**
Infinite bandwidth means there is no cut-off frequency. The gain is the same whether the input is d.c., low frequency a.c. or very high frequency a.c.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Look at the left-hand loop with the 1.5 V cell - point X sits between two resistors in series, so which type of circuit calculation gives the voltage at the junction?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot The Potential Divider**
The $1100\,\Omega$ and $400\,\Omega$ resistors are in series across $1.5\text{ V}$. Point X is their junction, with the bottom of the $400\,\Omega$ resistor at $0\text{ V}$ (earth).

Step 2: **Calculate $V_X$**
The voltage divides in proportion to resistance: $$V_X = V_{supply} \times \frac{R_{bottom}}{R_{top}+R_{bottom}}$$ $$V_X = 1.5 \times \frac{400}{1100+400} = 1.5 \times \frac{400}{1500} = 0.40\text{ V}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Identify the type of op-amp circuit from Fig. 7.1 - the input goes through a resistor to the inverting input with the non-inverting input earthed, so what controls the size of the amplification?
Hint 2: Work out the total resistance in the feedback loop by adding the thermistor resistance to the series fixed resistor, then think how it compares to the input resistor.
Hint 3: Use your input voltage of 0.40 V from (b)(i) together with the gain magnitude to find the output magnitude.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recognise Inverting Amplifier**
The + input is at $0\text{ V}$ (earth) and the signal at X feeds the - input via $96\text{ k}\Omega$. This is an inverting amplifier, so the magnitude of the voltage gain is: $$|G| = \frac{R_F}{R_{IN}}$$

Step 2: **Find $R_F$ and Gain**
The feedback path contains the thermistor in series with $100\text{ k}\Omega$: $$R_F = 360 + 100 = 460\text{ k}\Omega$$ $$|G| = \frac{460}{96} \approx 4.79$$

Step 3: **Calculate Output Magnitude**
Input voltage is $V_{IN} = V_X = 0.40\text{ V}$, so: $$|V_{OUT}| = |G| \times V_{IN} = \frac{460}{96} \times 0.40 \approx 1.9\text{ V}$$

parts.label: (b)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Recall what NTC means - how does the resistance of this type of thermistor respond when it gets hotter?
Hint 2: Link that resistance change to the feedback resistance and then to the gain formula you used in (b)(ii) to see what happens to the voltmeter reading.
parts.proper_answer: Resistance of NTC thermistor decreases with increasing temperature. Feedback resistance and magnitude of gain $R_F/R_{IN}$ decrease, so magnitude of $V_{OUT}$ decreases.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Effect On Thermistor**
NTC means negative temperature coefficient: hotter means more charge carriers are freed, so resistance falls. Thus $R_{thermistor}$ decreases.

Step 2: **Effect On Gain and Reading**
Since $$|G| = \frac{R_F}{R_{IN}}$$ and $R_F = R_{thermistor} + 100\text{ k}\Omega$, a smaller $R_{thermistor}$ gives a smaller $R_F$ and a smaller gain. With the same $V_{IN} = 0.40\text{ V}$, the output $$|V_{OUT}| = |G| \times V_{IN}$$ must decrease, so the voltmeter reading decreases.

parts.label: (b)(iv)
hints: Hint 1: Calculate what the output would need to be if gain were 12.5 with a 0.40 V input, and compare that value to the power supply voltages shown on the op-amp in Fig. 7.1.
parts.proper_answer: At gain 12.5, $V_{OUT}$ would be $5.0\text{ V}$ which equals the supply voltage, so the op-amp saturates and further increase in gain cannot increase $V_{OUT}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Saturation Limit**
With $V_{IN} = 0.40\text{ V}$: $$|V_{OUT}| = 12.5 \times 0.40 = 5.0\text{ V}$$ This equals the $+5.0\text{ V}$ and $-5.0\text{ V}$ supply rails. A real op-amp cannot output more than its supply, so it saturates at about $5\text{ V}$. Any larger gain still gives $5\text{ V}$, so temperature changes are no longer indicated.
